title: The Return of the Urban Beekeeper

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Twenty years ago, the idea of keeping bees on the roof of an office block would have struck most city planners as eccentric at best. Today, rooftop hives can be found above hotels, museums and even railway stations in many European capitals. In one major city, the number of registered urban hives roughly tripled over a single decade, and waiting lists for beekeeping courses now stretch for months.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The movement began largely as a response to alarming reports about the decline of pollinating insects in the countryside. Intensive agriculture, with its large single-crop fields and heavy use of pesticides, has reduced both the variety and the quantity of flowers available to bees. Cities, by contrast, offer a surprisingly rich mixture of parks, private gardens, street trees and window boxes, which flower at different times of the year and are often treated with fewer chemicals.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: However, ecologists have begun to question whether more hives automatically mean healthier bee populations. Honeybees are just one of hundreds of bee species, and most wild bees live alone rather than in large colonies. When too many honeybee colonies are placed in a small area, they may compete with wild species for the same limited supply of nectar and pollen. A study of one city centre found that the amount of pollen available per hive had fallen by almost a third as hive numbers rose.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For this reason, several local authorities now encourage residents to support pollinators in other ways. Rather than installing a hive, people are advised to plant flowers that bloom early in spring or late in autumn, when food is scarce, and to leave small areas of garden undisturbed so that ground-nesting bees can build their homes. Some councils have stopped mowing roadside verges during the summer months, allowing wild flowers to grow.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Supporters of urban beekeeping argue that its greatest value is educational. Hives on school roofs and in community gardens allow children and adults to observe insect behaviour at close range, and beekeepers often become enthusiastic campaigners for greener cities. Whether this benefit outweighs the risk to wild species is likely to depend on careful planning, including limits on the number of hives in any one district.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, sleep was regarded by many researchers as a passive state, a period in which the brain simply rested before the demands of the following day. That view has changed dramatically. Laboratory studies now suggest that sleep plays an active role in learning, helping the brain to strengthen some memories while allowing others to fade.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In a typical experiment, volunteers learn a list of word pairs or a sequence of finger movements in the evening and are tested the next morning. Those who sleep normally between learning and testing tend to recall more than volunteers who are kept awake for the same number of hours. Importantly, the advantage is not explained simply by tiredness: when the awake group is allowed to rest before the test, the sleeping group still performs better.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Different stages of sleep appear to support different kinds of memory. Deep, slow-wave sleep, which dominates the early part of the night, is closely linked to the consolidation of facts and events. Rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, which becomes more frequent towards morning, seems to be particularly important for practical skills and for emotional memories. Cutting a night short may therefore cost learners a disproportionate amount of REM sleep.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: These findings have obvious implications for students. Staying up late to revise may be less effective than many believe, because the material studied is less likely to be consolidated if sleep is lost. Some researchers recommend that learners review difficult material shortly before going to bed and then test themselves the next day, a routine that combines the benefits of sleep with those of active recall.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, scientists caution against drawing simple conclusions. Most studies involve small groups of young adults learning artificial tasks in unfamiliar laboratory conditions, and it is not yet clear how well the results apply to complex subjects such as mathematics or a foreign language. Long-term studies following students through an entire academic year are still rare.

title: How the Bicycle Changed Everyday Life

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The first machines that we would recognise as bicycles appeared in the early nineteenth century. They had no pedals: riders sat on a wooden frame and pushed themselves along with their feet. These 'running machines' were expensive and uncomfortable, and they were mostly a fashionable toy for wealthy young men.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Over the next sixty years, inventors added pedals, rubber tyres and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. The so-called safety bicycle, with two wheels of the same size, was far easier to ride than earlier designs, which often had an enormous front wheel. By the 1890s, factories were producing bicycles in large numbers, and prices fell sharply.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cheap bicycles changed the lives of ordinary working people. For the first time, many could live several kilometres from their workplace without paying for a train or a horse. Historians have noted that marriages between people from neighbouring villages became more common in some regions, perhaps because young people could now travel further to meet each other.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The bicycle also played a part in changing attitudes towards women. Cycling required practical clothing, and the long, heavy skirts of the time were gradually replaced by shorter skirts and loose trousers for riding. Many women described the freedom of being able to travel alone, and some campaigners for women's rights saw the bicycle as a symbol of independence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Today, after decades in which the car dominated city streets, the bicycle is enjoying a revival. Many cities are building separate cycle lanes, and electric bicycles are allowing older people and those with longer journeys to ride. For some planners, the humble bicycle once again represents the future of transport.

title: Tracking the Invisible: Microplastics in the Ocean

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When people imagine plastic pollution in the sea, they usually picture floating bottles and bags. Yet scientists increasingly believe that the most widespread form of plastic waste is almost invisible. Microplastics, defined as fragments smaller than five millimetres, have been found everywhere from the surface of the Arctic Ocean to sediments on the deepest parts of the sea floor.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some microplastics are manufactured at that size, such as the tiny beads once added to cosmetics. Most, however, are produced when larger items break down under the influence of sunlight, waves and temperature changes. Synthetic clothing is another significant source: every time clothes made from polyester or nylon are washed, thousands of microscopic fibres may be released into waste water, and many water treatment plants are not designed to capture particles that small.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Measuring the scale of the problem is surprisingly difficult. Researchers traditionally collected samples using nets dragged behind ships, but the mesh of these nets lets through the smallest particles. Recent studies using finer filters have found concentrations many times higher than earlier estimates, which suggests that the quantity of microplastics in the ocean may have been seriously underestimated.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consequences for marine life are still being investigated. Small animals such as plankton and shellfish can mistake microplastics for food, and laboratory experiments indicate that this may reduce their growth or ability to reproduce. Because these animals are eaten by larger species, scientists are concerned that particles may be passed along the food chain. Whether this poses a significant risk to human health is not yet known.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Several governments have banned microbeads in cosmetics, and some washing machine manufacturers are testing filters that catch fibres before they leave the machine. Most researchers agree, however, that the most effective long-term solution is to reduce the amount of plastic produced and to design products that are easier to recycle.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Before the 2020s, working from home was a privilege enjoyed by a small minority of employees, usually those in senior positions or in technology companies. Within a few years, it had become a normal arrangement for millions of office workers. Many organisations now operate a hybrid model, in which staff divide their week between the office and home.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For employees, the most frequently mentioned advantage is the time saved by not commuting. In large cities, a daily journey of more than an hour each way is common, and some workers report using the saved time for exercise, family life or additional work. Many also value the ability to concentrate without the interruptions of a busy open-plan office.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Employers' views are more mixed. Some companies have reduced their office space and saved considerable amounts on rent. Others worry that remote work makes it harder to train new staff, who traditionally learn by observing more experienced colleagues. Informal conversations in corridors and kitchens, which can lead to new ideas, are also difficult to recreate online.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are wider effects, too. Cafés and shops in business districts have lost customers, while those in residential suburbs have gained them. Some workers have moved away from expensive cities to smaller towns, which may help to spread economic activity more evenly. At the same time, not every job can be done remotely, and some researchers warn of a new divide between those who can choose where to work and those who cannot.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It is still too early to say what the long-term pattern will be. Surveys suggest that most employees who have experienced hybrid working would prefer to keep it, but many managers would like to see their teams in the office more often. The most successful arrangements may be those that are agreed openly between staff and employers, rather than imposed by either side.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support an extraordinary proportion of marine species. They also protect coastlines from storms and provide food and income for coastal communities. Over recent decades, however, rising sea temperatures have triggered repeated episodes of bleaching, in which stressed corals expel the microscopic algae that live in their tissues and supply most of their energy. If high temperatures persist, bleached corals may starve and die.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In response, marine scientists and volunteers have developed techniques that resemble gardening. Small fragments are cut from healthy corals and attached to underwater structures, sometimes called nurseries, where they can grow rapidly in favourable conditions. After several months, the fragments are transplanted onto damaged sections of reef. Some species grow surprisingly quickly when broken into pieces, a process that also occurs naturally after storms.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A newer approach focuses on resilience rather than numbers. Researchers have observed that certain individual corals survive heat waves that kill their neighbours. By identifying and breeding these individuals, scientists hope to produce populations better able to tolerate warmer water. Laboratory work has also explored whether exposing young corals to gradually increasing temperatures can strengthen their tolerance, a technique sometimes described as 'assisted evolution'.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics point out that restoration is expensive and operates on a tiny scale compared with the size of the world's reefs. Even the largest projects have restored only a few hectares, whereas some single reef systems extend for thousands of kilometres. There is also a concern that publicising restoration may create the false impression that damage to reefs can easily be reversed, reducing pressure on governments to cut the greenhouse gas emissions that cause ocean warming.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Most researchers in the field accept these criticisms but argue that restoration has a role to play alongside, not instead of, action on climate change. In their view, carefully targeted projects can protect reefs of particular economic or ecological value, preserve genetic diversity and buy time while emissions are reduced. They also stress the importance of involving local communities, whose knowledge of reefs is often detailed and whose support is essential for long-term success.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Parents raising children in two languages have often been given conflicting advice. In the past, some teachers and doctors warned that learning two languages at once would confuse young children and delay their speech. Today, most researchers reject this view, although they acknowledge that bilingual development follows its own patterns.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It is true that bilingual children may know fewer words in each individual language than children who speak only one. When the vocabulary of both languages is counted together, however, bilingual children typically know as many words as their monolingual peers, and sometimes more. Mixing languages within a sentence, which once worried parents, is now understood as a normal and often skilful feature of bilingual speech.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some studies have suggested that managing two languages gives children practice in controlling attention, because they must constantly select one language while ignoring the other. In several experiments, bilingual children performed better than monolingual children on tasks that required them to switch between rules. Other researchers have failed to reproduce these results, and the size of any advantage remains a matter of debate.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What is clearer is the social and cultural value of bilingualism. Children who speak the language of their grandparents can build closer family relationships and gain access to stories, songs and traditions that might otherwise be lost. In later life, two languages can widen career opportunities and make travel and study abroad easier.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Experts advise families to provide plenty of meaningful exposure to both languages. Many recommend that each parent consistently uses one language with the child, although other approaches, such as using one language at home and another outside, can also work well. The most important factor appears to be that children hear rich, varied language in situations they enjoy.

title: Farms That Grow Upwards

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a converted warehouse on the edge of a city, lettuce and herbs grow on shelves stacked eight levels high. There is no soil and no sunlight. Instead, the plants' roots sit in trays of nutrient-rich water, and coloured LED lights provide exactly the wavelengths the plants need. This is vertical farming, an approach that its supporters believe could transform the way cities are fed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The advantages are considerable. Because conditions are controlled, crops can be grown all year round regardless of the weather, and pests are rare enough that pesticides are seldom required. Water is recycled within the system, so vertical farms typically use a small fraction of the water needed in open fields. Locating farms close to consumers also reduces transport distances and allows food to be sold within hours of harvesting.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The greatest challenge is energy. Replacing sunlight with artificial lighting requires large amounts of electricity, and climate control adds further costs. As a result, vertical farms have so far focused on crops that grow quickly and sell at high prices, such as salad leaves, herbs and strawberries. Staple crops such as wheat and rice, which require large areas and fetch low prices, are not currently economical to grow indoors.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Several high-profile vertical farming companies have closed in recent years, often because rising electricity prices made their products too expensive. Others have survived by building farms next to sources of cheap renewable energy, or by selling their technology to traditional growers. Researchers are also developing more efficient lights and plant varieties bred specifically for indoor conditions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Few experts believe that vertical farms will replace conventional agriculture. A more realistic expectation is that they will supply a growing share of fresh produce to cities, particularly in places where land is scarce or the climate is harsh, while fields continue to provide most of the world's calories.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Much of what we do each day is not the result of careful decisions but of habit. We brush our teeth, check our phones and take the same route to work without really thinking about it. Psychologists estimate that a large share of daily behaviour is repeated in the same place every day, which suggests that habits shape our lives far more than we realise.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A habit usually begins with a cue, such as a time of day, a place or a feeling. The cue triggers a routine, and the routine is followed by a reward that makes us more likely to repeat it. Over time, the link between cue and routine becomes automatic. This explains why it can be so hard to stop checking a phone: the sound of a notification acts as a cue, and the small pleasure of a new message works as a reward.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Forming a new habit takes longer than many people expect. In one well-known study, participants chose a simple healthy behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water after breakfast, and recorded whether they did it each day. On average, it took more than two months before the behaviour felt automatic, although the time varied greatly between individuals and between behaviours.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Experts suggest several strategies for building habits. Linking a new behaviour to an existing routine, for example reading for ten minutes after dinner, provides a reliable cue. Starting with a very small version of the behaviour reduces the effort required. Missing a single day does not seem to matter much, so people should not give up after one failure.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of their history, museums have been places that people had to visit in person. Objects were kept behind glass, and information was limited to small printed labels. Over the past two decades, digital technology has begun to change both how collections are displayed and who can see them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Many major museums have photographed their collections and published the images online, often free of charge. A student on another continent can now examine an ancient manuscript in greater detail than a visitor standing in front of the display case. Some institutions have also released their images for anyone to reuse, which has led to new designs, educational materials and research projects.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Inside the galleries, technology is changing the visitor experience. Interactive screens allow people to explore the history of an object, while audio guides on smartphones offer stories told by curators, artists and members of local communities. Some museums use virtual reality to show how a ruined building may have looked when it was new.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes these changes. Some critics argue that screens distract visitors from the real objects and turn museums into entertainment venues. Others worry that smaller museums cannot afford expensive technology and may fall further behind well-funded national institutions. Digitising a large collection can take many years and requires specialist staff.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Surveys of visitors suggest that online collections have not reduced the desire to see objects in person; in some cases, seeing an object online makes people more eager to visit. Many museum directors therefore see digital and physical access as complementary rather than competing.

title: Riverside Community Centre: Information for New Members

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Welcome to Riverside Community Centre. The centre is open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. at weekends. It is closed on public holidays. Members must show their membership card at reception each time they visit.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The swimming pool is available for lane swimming every morning until 11 a.m. Family swimming sessions take place on Saturday and Sunday afternoons, and children under eight must be accompanied by an adult in the water. Swimming caps are not compulsory but are recommended for people with long hair.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Evening classes run in three terms throughout the year. Popular courses include beginner's photography, conversational Spanish and healthy cooking on a budget. Places are limited, so members are advised to book online at least one week before a course begins. Members receive a twenty per cent discount on all course fees.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Lockers are available free of charge, but members need to bring their own padlock. The centre cannot accept responsibility for valuables left in the changing rooms. Lost property is kept at reception for one month.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If you would like to suggest a new activity or report a problem, please complete a feedback form at reception or email the centre manager. We aim to reply to all messages within five working days.

title: Starting Work at Greenway Logistics: Staff Guide

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: All new employees attend an induction day on their first Monday. The induction covers health and safety procedures, the company's computer systems and an introduction to your team. Please bring photographic identification and your bank details so that the payroll department can set up your salary payments.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Standard working hours are 8.30 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday, with a one-hour lunch break. Staff may apply for flexible hours after completing a three-month probation period. Requests should be discussed with your line manager and confirmed in writing by the human resources department.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: If you are unable to work because of illness, you must telephone your line manager before 9 a.m. on the first day of absence. Text messages and emails are not acceptable as a first notification. For absences of more than five days, a doctor's note is required.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Annual leave entitlement is twenty-five days per year, plus public holidays. Leave requests should normally be made at least two weeks in advance, and no more than ten consecutive working days may be taken without the approval of a senior manager. Unused leave cannot usually be carried over into the following year.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The staff car park is free, but spaces are limited and are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis. Employees who cycle to work can use the secure bicycle shelter and the showers on the ground floor. The company also offers interest-free loans to help staff buy annual public transport passes.
